changelog_v2_4_1: Records a commit-citation correction: a CTO order cited 'manifest v2.4.0, commit 4e1f550' -- 4e1f550 is v2.2.0, three mandates earlier (see version_history above for the real chain). Freezing state by citing that commit would freeze a stale version; recorded here so the correction is durable, not just conversational. Registers H1_from_M15_v2 under context_derived_htf.entries (hash 524977d0...f660, 49,580 bars, independently verified directly against the physical file, cross-checked against Data Acquisition's DATA_ACQUISITION_FINAL_REPORT.md line 140 -- not copied from any relayed message), with an explicit classification_delimitation and governance_note disclosing that this is the first registration in the project driven by an operational need (unblocking Research Lab's mstrat context guard) rather than by the data reaching a qualification threshold on its own -- accepted only because it reuses the already-validated H4/D1 mechanism unchanged, stays permanently distinct from the native H1 entry, and is explicitly NOT a template for future convenience-driven classifications. Promotes H4/D1/H1_from_M15_v2 status from VALIDATED to the more specific CONTEXT_DERIVED_VALIDATED (matching provenance_key exactly, avoiding confusion with base-timeframe VALIDATED). Statistician ratifies hashes only, not rule-conformance (which rests on Data Acquisition's own 28/28-passing test suite) -- stated explicitly, again, as a real structural gap being addressed separately (CROSS_VERIFICATION_SPEC_v1.0), not a weakness papered over.
changelog_v2_7_43: A candidate that had been declared untestable came back reformulated, and adversarial review passed it with a sharp caveat: the fix moves the problem rather than removing it. The old version demanded that a weekly high be traded short only while the market trend was down, and since a high is only reached by rallying toward it, the two demands contradicted each other and left seven usable events. Dropping the trend filter removes that collapse, but the contradiction does not disappear -- it relocates into the trade direction itself, where it is now measurable rather than merely fatal. Checking the inputs before writing anything produced two corrections. The population figure everyone was quoting, including this division, counts all weekly levels while the policy only trades weeks that ran their full length; the real number is 258, not 275. And the premise that the session results were still being computed turned out to be stale -- they were already finished and sitting in the results file, which meant the sorting rule fixed last round could be applied immediately rather than waited on. A prediction made before any of this data existed was that the shorter the period a level is drawn from, the less it suffers from this contradiction. The middle measurement needed to check it was missing, so it was taken: session 33.6 percent, daily 26.6 percent, weekly 2.2 percent. The ordering holds for the third time, but the shape of the claim was wrong and is corrected here -- the decline is gentle from session to daily and then falls off a cliff at weekly, not gradual as implied. Alongside it sits something more interesting: the rate at which price actually reaches these levels is nearly identical at all three scales, within a point of each other despite a thirty-five-fold difference in period length, which rules out the obvious alternative explanation that longer-period levels are simply too far away to matter. The direction test itself could not be copied from the sibling candidate that already has one. At a midpoint, both directions have somewhere to aim; at a weekly high, the fade direction has a target below but the opposite direction has nothing above it, so the two arms would have differed in how they exit as well as which way they point, and no difference could have been attributed to direction. The matched construction specified here shares entry and risk distance and lets both arms run to the same deadline, leaving the sign of the position as the only difference. Quantifying the reviewer point about selling into a rally: at weekly scale the market is running against this trade in ninety-eight cases out of a hundred, which makes the two arms unequally informative and forces an interpretation to be committed in advance -- in particular that the opposite arm winning would not license quietly rebranding the idea as a trend-following one, since that is a new hypothesis chosen after seeing the answer. Without that commitment every possible outcome would have had a ready explanation, which is another way of saying the test would have proved nothing. The suggestion to score the three level-based candidates as their own group was declined, because a smaller group means a more forgiving bar, and applying it to the three most promising candidates is the same favouritism refused earlier under a different name. The observation was kept and re-homed where it is genuinely useful. Applying the sorting rule to everything now finished produced a result worth stating plainly rather than burying: two candidates already inside the tested pool meet the standard for being shelved as losers, and one of them is among the four cleared for live demonstration on criteria this division wrote. Removing them was refused on the ground that shrinking the pool makes life easier for everything left in it -- the same trap, again -- so the pool only ever grows, and the demonstration question was passed upward rather than decided here. Also corrected: the fear that a growing pool crushes everything rests on treating the correction as harsher than it is, since only the strongest single result faces the full penalty. Finally, this division declared its own arrears -- three candidates that cleared review and testing without a plan, including the one cited repeatedly as a cautionary tale, which the rule sends forward anyway because its record is mixed and the rule is applied as written even when the outcome is unwelcome.
changelog_v2_7_42: A governance question with real teeth: twelve candidates cleared adversarial review without a test plan, six of them already screened and every one of those losing money -- the worst by a wide margin. Writing formal plans for all of them would widen the pool of simultaneous attempts and tighten the bar for every candidate, including the ones actually worth pursuing. Reading the screening file rather than the summary turned up something the framing had flattened: the six are not one group. Five lost heavily across large samples. The sixth produced seven trades in fifteen years. Seven. That is not a candidate that failed; it is one that never got the chance to be judged, and calling it a failure would confuse having no evidence with having evidence against. Its design requires two conditions to coincide, and requiring coincidences is exactly what shrinks a population to nothing -- the same shape as a recent case where the apparent deadness turned out to be the framing rather than the idea. So the sorting rule has three outcomes rather than two: clearly and consistently losing across every year and every market period, in which case the sign is structural and a formal test would only confirm what is already plain; too little data to judge at all, which is a different verdict entirely; or genuinely mixed, which earns a full test plan. On that basis five are shelved as losing, one as unjudgeable, and none needs a plan. A check nobody asked for was added: since a pending revision to assumed trading costs could in principle rescue a marginal loser, the arithmetic was run, and none of the five comes close to breaking even -- with the two nearest the line named in advance as the ones to look at first if that revision turns out larger than expected, so that revisiting later cannot be a matter of convenience. Shelved, importantly, does not mean disproven: none was ever formally tested, so none has been refuted, and any of them may come back if the evidence changes, at the cost of a slot at that point. The heart of the answer is separating two counts that get conflated. One tracks how many ideas were formally tested, and it governs how strict the evidence bar must be. The other tracks how many were examined at all, and it exists so nobody can later claim a flattering success rate. Shelving losers cannot distort the first, because the safeguard in question limits how many false discoveries get announced, and something never tested announces nothing. What shelving quietly WOULD distort is the second -- which is exactly why the exploration count stays on the record even though it never affects the threshold. That dissolves the dilemma: there was never a need to choose between testing everything and hiding the discards. For the six still being screened, the sorting rule is fixed now, before their numbers arrive, so it cannot be bent to fit them. Their test plans carry the usual requirement that a narrower variant must beat its broader parent on the very same occasions rather than beating nothing at all -- and for one of them, whose entire trade direction rests on an assumption its author explicitly flagged as unproven, the comparison is against that assumption reversed, since otherwise a good result might come from the level mattering at all rather than from the rule being right.
changelog_v2_7_41: A gatekeeping rule for the one class of price levels that reviewers had banned outright: the ones that persist indefinitely until touched, which pile up until somewhere between ninety and nearly two hundred of them are live at once. The objection was not merely that this is a lot. It was that with that many levels the price is always sitting near one, so the claim that price reacts to these levels can never be shown wrong -- it is true by saturation rather than by evidence. That distinction turned out to decide the whole design, before any data was touched. The obvious fixes -- keep the nearest handful, or the most recent handful -- reduce the count but leave the deeper problem completely intact, because a rule that always hands back a fixed number of levels guarantees price is always near one. It hides the saturation rather than removing it. What is actually required is a rule that can hand back NOTHING, because the possibility of no level being in play is precisely what makes the claim capable of failing. That rules out ranking and points to a distance cutoff. Limiting by age was set aside for a different reason: a short limit would simply turn this class back into the ordinary short-lived one, which defeats its entire purpose, while a long limit constrains nothing -- whereas distance keeps the idea intact, since a level far from current price genuinely does not matter right now but becomes relevant again if price comes back to it. The cutoff was fixed in advance, with its main value borrowed from a measure this lab already uses everywhere as its unit of risk rather than picked to suit this problem, and with two alternatives written down beforehand purely as sensitivity checks. It reads only the previous bar's closing price and volatility, both finished before the current bar begins, which is what makes it usable in real time rather than only in hindsight. The bar for calling it effective was set by taking an order of magnitude off the already-published counts, rather than by inventing a target. Then it was measured across the full fifteen years, and the unfiltered figures reproduced the reviewers' numbers exactly, confirming the same thing was being filtered. The main pre-chosen setting passed comfortably: the typical count drops to zero and the worst case from one hundred eighty-eight to six. Because it passed, nothing had to be re-picked afterwards. The falsifiability question was answered numerically for the first time: before filtering, the share of moments with no level nearby was zero percent -- literally never -- and afterwards it is roughly five in six, so the claim now has something it can get wrong. A second measurement checked the obvious worry that such a harsh cut would leave nothing to study, and it does not: just over half the touch events survive, which is structural rather than lucky, since a level about to be touched is necessarily already close to price, so what gets discarded is the far-away levels that were never going to be reached -- the dilution itself. Finally, and stated plainly rather than buried: this does not solve the volume problem. The surviving event count sits in the same range as the three largest losses this project has recorded, all of which came from having too many zones. The filter fixes what was asked -- saturation and testability -- and nothing more, so anything built on this class still needs its own selectivity and must report how many trades it generates before reporting how they performed.
changelog_v2_7_40: Three missing trigger-detectors specified, so that three candidates which already had both their entry logic and their risk logic written could finally become testable -- what they lacked was never the exit rule, only the event that starts the trade. All three are built by copying conventions that already exist and are already ratified, rather than inventing parallel ones, which is the approach that got the most recent similar piece of work through adversarial review on the first attempt. The most valuable part concerns the weekly-levels candidate. An earlier survey had found it produced only six usable instances across fifteen years, which looked like a fatal problem, and the request was to say whether building the detector was even worth it before anyone spent the effort. Rather than guess, the funnel was measured directly: of five hundred and seventy-two weekly levels produced, two hundred and seventy-five were actually reached by price -- which is a perfectly healthy rate, just under half -- and only six of those also had the trend filter pointing the right way. Since that reproduces the original figure and its regime-by-regime breakdown exactly, it is the same population being taken apart rather than a different one. So the detector was never the bottleneck: the filter was. And the reason is structural rather than bad luck. Price can only reach last week's high by rallying up to it, but the trade that level implies is a short, which demands that the broader trend be falling -- the two requirements are close to mutually exclusive, because arriving at a weekly extreme generally means the trend is running the other way. The raw counts show it starkly: the highs were reached one hundred and forty-seven times and qualified twice. This generalises into a prediction worth keeping: for any level defined as a previous period's extreme, being reached and being trend-aligned-for-a-reversal pull against each other, and the conflict gets worse the longer the period -- mild at daily scale, severe at weekly -- which implies the newer session-based levels should suffer least of all, and that is cheap to check. The practical upshot saves the requested round, though not in the expected direction: build the detector, because it works and yields two hundred and seventy-five usable events, but rewrite the candidate that was supposed to use it, because the problem was always in how that candidate was framed. Three ways to reframe it are laid out without picking one, since that belongs to the division that owns it. For the other two detectors: gap reactions copy an existing three-stage reaction ladder, since a gap left by a jump in price is the same kind of object as the gaps already handled, and the rejection stage reuses an existing signature rather than adding a fourth definition of the same idea. The overlap-zone detector required more care, because that object genuinely has no side of its own -- so the detector reports only which side price entered from and leaves direction to be supplied, explicitly and on the record, by whatever strategy uses it. Finally, weeks cut short by data boundaries are kept rather than silently dropped, but must be reported apart from whole weeks, because an extreme measured over fewer days is systematically less extreme, therefore closer to price, therefore reached more often -- mixing them would quietly overstate how often these levels get touched.
changelog_v2_7_39: Two things at once: the formal sign-off on the two structural detection modules that have been blocked for months, and a design for a new family of price levels built on trading sessions. On the sign-off, the measurements behind it were checked rather than taken on trust, and all three matched exactly -- roughly two in five candles that broke anything broke more than one thing, one candle cleared twenty-four levels at once, and five hundred and forty-two events had been vanishing entirely. A cross-check worth noting: the increase in total events under the repaired logic equals that vanishing count to the unit, which independently confirms the earlier prediction that the old logic was destroying events rather than merely postponing them, and that nothing else inflated the total. One reassurance was accepted but its reasoning tightened: the claim that four downstream users are unaffected is correct, but not for the reason first given -- filtering by event type does not settle it, because two events of the SAME type can now land on one candle, and the comparison used to pick between them cannot separate them, so list order silently decides. The real protection is the ordering rule chosen earlier specifically to preserve existing behaviour, which means that rule is now structural rather than cosmetic: change it and four strategies quietly start referencing a different price level. It is frozen with a test to enforce it. Three items stay open, none blocking. The first is contradictory signals landing together on one candle -- ruled not a fault of the detector but an honest report of a genuinely self-contradictory market structure, so hiding one side would conceal something real and recreate exactly the artefact just removed; both are reported, and any consumer that receives both must either decline to act (the default) or declare its own rule openly rather than burying one in code, with the frequency to be measured so that calling it harmless becomes a fact. The second is four missing tests, specified as acceptance criteria, with the two that matter most called out: one that turns the ordering rule into an enforced guarantee, and one that checks nothing is lost or double-counted across a whole segment, which is precisely the property the old defect violated and that nothing was checking. The third is re-running three strategies whose results depended on the repaired detector -- confirmed as fixing an execution error rather than taking a second swing at the same data, since the idea being tested never changed and the detector was simply missing events that idea always covered. To keep that honest rather than convenient, the scope, the metrics, and the rule that the new numbers replace the old ones in either direction including a worse one are all committed to in advance. On session levels, three levels per completed session are specified by copying the conventions of the existing previous-day levels exactly rather than inventing parallel ones. The building block is kept general, with any narrowing left to the strategies that use it, on the established principle that shared infrastructure must not quietly encode one hypothesis. Two competing lifetimes are specified as genuinely separate things to be measured separately, and the accumulating one carries a hard precondition drawn from a failure already paid for: an earlier construction generated over eighteen thousand trades and lost money before anyone noticed there were simply too many zones, so the count of simultaneously live levels must be measured before anything is built on it. Finally, a distinction that would otherwise have slipped through: the midpoint of a session is not the same kind of object as its high or low, because orders rest beyond extremes but nothing rests at a midpoint -- so it needs its own definition of being touched, it carries no inherent direction, and it must never be averaged together with the other two.
changelog_v2_7_38: A timing repair to the structure-break detector, and a correction to the assumption that nothing already measured depends on it. The reviewers had found that when several old structural levels are all taken out by one decisive close, the detector reports them one per bar instead of together -- so the oldest of five gets recorded an hour late on a fifteen-minute chart, even though price cleared it in the very first candle. The decision from above was that everything broken by a given candle should be reported on that candle, with entry still on the following one. Writing that out precisely turned up a second cause nobody had named: not only does the detector track just one level of each kind at a time, it also actively suppresses a change-of-character reading whenever a plain continuation reading fires on the same candle. The instruction as worded covers both, so both are fixed, but the second is called out explicitly because it changes a long-standing precedence that the worked example did not touch -- better surfaced for the reviewers to attack than slipped in quietly. It also emerged that the suppression was not merely delaying those readings: if price slipped back on the next candle, the suppressed reading was lost for good, so the repair actually produces MORE events in that situation, which is not a change to the agreed counting rule but the belated delivery of what that rule always said. On the question of what order to list several events sharing one candle, the answer turned out to matter for a consumer that already exists: a helper elsewhere in the codebase picks the earliest match by comparing bar numbers, and that comparison simply cannot separate events that now share the same bar number, so whichever is listed first silently wins. The order chosen is the one that preserves current behaviour -- most recent level first, matching what the existing code already picks -- so the change stays confined to timing rather than quietly also changing which level gets referenced. The deeper question it exposes, whether the level that counts should be the nearest or the furthest of several cleared at once, is flagged as belonging to whoever owns those strategies rather than being settled by an ordering default. The most important correction concerns the claim that nothing needs re-running. That holds for the candidate policies, which genuinely touch only an inert helper -- but a separate strategy module does call this detector in four places, and it uses break timing to decide whether a setup even qualifies within a fixed window, so a late reading can push a setup in or out of eligibility rather than merely shifting its entry. Three previously-measured strategy results therefore depend on this after all, while one prominent rejected result was checked and confirmed not to. Rather than overstate that, the frequency of the stacking situation was never tested and remains unknown, so the measurement is required first and any re-run decision waits on it -- and such a re-run would be a correction to execution, not a fresh attempt at the same data.
changelog_v2_7_37: The first time anyone actually paid a trading cost on a live practice account rather than assuming one, and the question of whether that overturns a long series of negative verdicts -- because the assumed cost is very nearly the only thing that killed most of them. Nothing is overturned here; a single trade settles nothing, and that is agreed at the outset. What is done instead is to establish what would have to be true, and how it would have to be measured, before any of it could be revisited. The first step was checking where the assumed figure came from, and it turns out not to have been measured at all: half of it was a spread taken from a stated range, and the other half was slippage set equal to spread purely by convention. That matters enormously, because it splits one apparent fourfold error into two quite different problems. The spread half can be watched directly and cheaply, and the new observation speaks to it. The slippage half cannot be observed by watching quotes at all -- it only ever shows up when real orders are filled, at real size, during exactly the fast-moving conditions in which every one of these strategies happens to trade. A single calm, tiny trade showing no slippage tells us almost nothing about that half, and it is the half that never had any evidence behind it. It was also worth noting that the spread seen sits at the quiet end of the range originally described, which is what a calmly-timed sample looks like, and that a spread this narrow usually means an account type that bills separately -- something to confirm rather than assume, since it could mean the figure quoted is not the whole cost. On how to sample, the quantity that actually matters is not the average spread across the day but the average cost at the moments these strategies would trade -- and those moments cluster in exactly the turbulent conditions where spreads widen, so sampling evenly through the clock would flatter the answer. Watching continuously is still the right way to gather the raw material, but the labels have to be recorded alongside so the answer can be reweighted toward the moments that count. The sharpest practical point is that readings taken every thirty seconds are nearly copies of one another, so counting them as independent evidence would produce false confidence -- what counts is distinct days, not readings, which honestly means weeks or months of patient collection rather than an afternoon. On which conclusions could actually be revisited, the reason offered for not simply recalculating turned out to be wrong, though the conclusion was right: the gross figures are arithmetically clean, but the assumed cost quietly determined which trades were eligible to be counted in the first place, so changing it changes the population rather than just the arithmetic. Most importantly, the same standard applied earlier when a favourable argument was turned down is applied again here: a measurement taken in today's market establishes today's costs, not those of a decade ago, and accepting that inference now while having rejected it before would be a double standard -- so the honest position is that this reopens nothing historical by itself, however encouraging it looks. Sorting the past verdicts by why they actually failed rather than by whether the news is welcome, some were killed squarely by cost and are genuine candidates; one was killed because its underlying advantage was never reliably positive in the first place, and a smaller cost cannot manufacture something that was not there; and the one genuinely positive finding in the whole line never involved cost at all and is therefore untouched in either direction. Finally, whether cost should be treated as a fixed amount or one that grows with market activity is left to the data, with the deciding test written down in advance -- and doing so deliberately puts an earlier explanation of this lab's own at risk, since one plausible outcome would refute it outright.
changelog_v2_7_36: Practice-account measurement rules for three more pilot strategies, following a second round of adversarial review that cleared all three on the axes that matter for trust -- no peeking ahead, no circular reasoning, nothing tunable that could have been quietly fitted -- while flagging that each is silent on the same execution details the first pilot had to have pinned down. That existing rulebook is applied word for word rather than reinvented, along with the same three settings the strategies had handed over, decided once with the reasoning stated once instead of repeated three times. On the breakout strategy, the review's concern about a position potentially being held for weeks turned out to understate the problem. The strategy's backstop for closing a trade that never meets an opposing move is the end of a data block -- but a block is a bookkeeping artefact of the historical dataset, a labelled stretch of past market conditions. On an account trading forward in real time there is no current block and no end of one to arrive at, so that backstop never fires at all: the trade simply has no time limit whatsoever. This is the same trap already identified once before, where something knowable only in hindsight cannot be used as a live instruction. Inventing a replacement was declined as out of bounds and handed back to the division that owns the risk design; what is imposed instead is measurement, using length scales this lab already derived for other purposes rather than any newly chosen number, plus counts of overnight and weekend exposure. On the gap-reaction strategy -- flagged as the most exposed of the three because its exit levels are the two edges of a single gap that can be arbitrarily narrow -- two further consequences were worked out that the review had not drawn. The first is that the safety floor on position sizing, when it bites, pushes the exit level past the very boundary that gave it its meaning, so on narrow gaps the floor does not merely shrink the position, it quietly voids the strategy's own stated reasoning for where that level sits. The second is arithmetic: because entry sits at the gap's midpoint, the distance to safety and the distance to profit start out equal, but the floor stretches only the first of them while the second stays put -- so precisely on the narrow gaps where the floor bites, the reward-to-risk balance collapses systematically rather than occasionally. Those trades must therefore be reported as their own group, since averaging them together with the rest would bury a structurally disadvantaged population under a single figure. A third point reframes something that had been treated as routine bookkeeping into a genuine warning light: when a single bar covers both exit levels at once, the outcome is decided by the conservative tie-breaking rule rather than by anything the market did, and on narrow gaps that will happen often -- so the share of outcomes decided by the rule must be reported next to the share decided by observation, with the plain warning that a result dominated by the former teaches very little about the idea being tested. On the combination strategy, whose wider protective level makes it immune to the previous problem, the mirror-image issue was noted: that same width can leave less to gain than to lose. Since both figures are known the moment the trade opens, this becomes a recorded quantity per trade rather than a retrospective observation -- but imposing a rule that refuses such trades was declined, as that would be adding an entry condition rather than measuring one. Finally, because this strategy borrows its exit from one sibling and sits inside another's territory, the existing requirement to prove it adds something over its parts was extended to cover the risk side too, so that any apparent advantage cannot come merely from having a wider protective level. The reviewers' condition on the most exposed strategy is carried word for word: without demonstrable enforcement, it does not trade.
changelog_v2_7_35: Two of the candidate strategies turned out to be pointed at the same price level from opposite sides -- one betting the level holds and price turns away, the other betting it gives way and price drives through -- and on the specific bars where the level is struck with real force, both fire at once, in opposite directions. The reviewers noticed the boundary between them is lopsided: the break strategy carefully steps aside when the evidence favours a turn, but the turn strategy has no matching clause, so on every forceful break it is left holding the wrong side by construction. Three ways out were offered, and the choice made was to combine two of them rather than pick one, because the question underneath is really two questions with different right answers. Judged as science, the contested bars are not a fair sample at all -- they are the bars on which the turn strategy's own premise is contradicted by the very bar being scored -- so the clean measurement leaves them out. Judged as operations, the strategy as written really would take those trades, so leaving them out would describe something other than what actually happens. Both are therefore measured, and the gap between the two numbers is itself the honest price of the missing clause -- which is what the third option asked for, obtained as a side effect of doing the first properly rather than in place of it, and costing no additional data since it is the same events sorted two ways. The weakness of this choice is stated rather than glossed: what gets tested is no longer quite what gets traded, and that is precisely why the second measurement is required rather than encouraged. Changing the strategy itself was declined on two grounds -- it belongs to another division, and it would tear up a chain of approvals that strategy has already passed, on the strength of a problem nobody has yet measured. There is also a quieter technical reason the chosen route is the right one, surfaced here rather than in the review: when two strategies hold opposite positions on shared bars, their results move against each other, and the standard method already committed to for keeping false positives in check across many simultaneous tests is only proven safe when results move together or independently, not against each other. Keeping them on separate bars removes the shared ground entirely and keeps that method valid; accepting the overlap would have forced a substitute roughly two and a half times harsher, punishing five other candidates that have nothing to do with the dispute. A live consequence of all this was also caught: the practice-account rules written for the turn strategy a step earlier were settled before this problem surfaced, meaning that account would quietly absorb the losing side of every forceful break. Rather than alter the strategy, the contested trades must now be reported as their own clearly-labelled group, with every figure shown both including and excluding them, so the cost is observed on the real account rather than discovered afterward. Separately, a second candidate was confirmed to sit entirely inside an existing one -- every one of its setups is an existing setup plus an extra condition -- so the fair question is whether that extra condition adds anything over the simpler version on exactly the same occasions, not whether it beats random. A third flagged item was resolved without escalation, since the strategy's own written rules already demand the behaviour twice over and only the shorthand expression was loose. Finally, the running count of how many independent attempts have been made against the same historical data was corrected upward from four to seven, an amendment to an earlier decision of the Statistician's own: all seven come from one continuous production line over one body of data, and keeping separate small tallies per batch would be exactly the trap that keeping a tally is meant to prevent. The correction is free because nothing has actually been run yet, and urgent because four of them were cleared to run while this was being written -- so the corrected threshold has to be in place before the first result, not applied to it afterward.
changelog_v2_7_34: The measurement rules for the one pilot policy cleared to run on a practice account with real fills -- how it gets scored, and what the execution software has to guarantee before a single order goes out. The risk approach itself is deliberately left alone: it belongs to another division, it is already frozen, and touching it was explicitly out of bounds. What was in bounds is everything around it. The adversarial reviewers had passed the approach on every axis they attack -- no peeking at the future, no circular reasoning, and unusually, nothing tunable at all, which is the strongest possible evidence nobody quietly fitted it to past results -- but flagged three ways the surrounding machinery could still misbehave once real money mechanics are involved. All three are turned into hard preconditions with specific fields the software must produce per trade, so that compliance can be checked rather than asserted. The first concerns a single price bar wide enough to contain both the exit-at-a-loss level and the take-profit level, where which one happened first is genuinely unknowable without finer data. Rather than let the software guess favorably, the existing house rule gets extended consistently to all three such collisions the reviewers listed -- not just the one they emphasized -- always resolving against the trade. Care was taken not to overcorrect: the harshest category, throwing the trade out entirely, stays reserved for the cases the house rule actually reserves it for, since widening it would have quietly discarded perfectly valid trades and biased results the other way. The second concerns position size: because size is set by dividing a fixed risk amount by the distance to the exit level, an unusually close exit level produces an enormous position. The zero-distance case was already guarded, but the nearly-zero case was not, and on a real account that is a live hazard rather than a rounding curiosity. The existing house floor is applied verbatim and, importantly, size must be computed from the floored distance rather than the raw one. The third turned out not to need a new rule at all, only a precision about when measurement starts -- checking for the profit target strictly from the bar after entry onward makes any earlier same-day visit to that price irrelevant by construction. Three loose ends the policy had handed over were also settled, after catching and correcting a direction error in an earlier draft that had them pointing the wrong way. The minimum-trades figure is set, but its description is corrected: it had been called a statistical-power threshold, and it cannot be one, because power only means something relative to a test being run, and this exercise deliberately runs none -- it is a threshold below which figures are withheld entirely rather than shown with a warning label, and crossing it grants no credibility whatsoever. No market-condition filter is applied, for a reason specific to this setting rather than a general preference: the condition labels are assigned looking backward and simply cannot be known while trading forward, so filtering on them could not be carried out honestly -- they stay a way of grouping results afterward, nothing more. And the treatment of trading costs marks the real difference between this and every measurement this lab has done before: here costs are observed rather than assumed, so actual spread and slippage must be captured on every fill and reconciled openly against the figure the lab has always modeled. Noted, without overreaching, that a persistent gap between the two would say something about every historical result produced here -- and equally noted that drawing that conclusion would require its own separate check, not an inference smuggled in through this one. The reviewers' own closing condition is carried word for word: if the software cannot be shown to enforce all three guarantees, the policy does not trade. And stated without hedging: none of this is validation. No significance figure is computed, no formal claim is tested, nothing is promoted, and a good-looking outcome here does not even earn the status of something worth registering later -- it is inconclusive by construction.
changelog_v2_7_33: The first real trigger under the operational-mode commitment made just one step earlier -- checking again within the same sitting, exactly as promised, turned up four candidates that had cleared the adversarial-review gate while the previous check was still being written up. All four get a full test plan today: a fixed number of independent looks this whole batch counts as against the running total, a plainly stated question each one has to answer before it counts as anything, the bar for calling that answer real rather than noise, a firm commitment that no held-back data gets touched, a two-stage forward check using period boundaries already settled rather than an invented split, and every known weak spot written down rather than left for someone to discover later. All four count as one batch for that running total, not four separate ones, because all four came out of the same production pass over the same historical data and were reviewed together in the same sitting -- one of the four gets a differently-shaped question later on, but that doesn't earn it a lower price of admission, since the correction that governs how many chances get taken cares about how many questions get asked, not how each one happens to be phrased. The first candidate, a prior-day-level reaction, gets its plain question plus a proper matched comparison borrowed directly from a testing pattern this project already built and trusts for exactly this purpose -- a same-time-of-day, same-distance-from-level control, not a bare zero. It also carries forward, as a limitation rather than something patched over with an invented correction, that this exact construction was reportedly one of nine similar ideas looked at before landing here -- accepted as a real caveat rather than quietly assigning it a made-up penalty with no way to check the number. A separate check for how much this candidate's own trigger set overlaps with a related one later in the batch gets required as description, not as a test that would need its own separate accounting. One more flagged concern named for this candidate doesn't have an obvious connection to how it's actually built, so rather than guess at what it means, it gets handed forward for the reviewer who raised it to clarify. The second candidate, a volatility-squeeze-into-breakout idea, carries forward its own already-disclosed weak spot -- the exact threshold defining a quiet market was a judgment call, not derived from first principles, and that stays true regardless of today's work rather than being re-argued here. The third candidate, a gap-fill reaction, needed nothing extra -- the reviewer flagged it as the cleanest of the four, and the plain question applies as-is. The fourth, a combination requiring two of the earlier ideas to agree at once, needed real care: because every single instance where this one fires is also, by definition, an instance where each of its two ingredients fires on its own, the honest question isn't whether the combination beats doing nothing -- it's whether requiring both actually beats whichever single ingredient already does better, checked on the exact same handful of moments rather than each ingredient's own larger, different set of moments. A same-timing-tolerance setting gets fixed at its strictest, same-instant value as the main version, with two slightly looser settings written down in advance purely to check sensitivity -- decided before anyone looks at outcomes, not picked afterward because it happened to look better. Stated plainly for all four together, not buried: none of this can actually be run yet, because the entirely separate question of how a position gets sized and exited hasn't been answered for any of them, and that gap is its own request, not something resolved by today's test-design work. Handed to Validation Engine, with the queue entries updated to show the plan is done and execution is waiting on that separate risk-sizing answer.
changelog_v2_7_32: An instruction to stop waiting for a fresh order each time and instead act the moment any candidate reaches a specific pass mark from the adversarial review stage, working through them one after another without pausing in between. Accepted that as the standing way of operating going forward, but was upfront about a real limit rather than pretending it away: responding turn by turn to whoever is present means there's no way to keep working unattended in the gaps between conversations without a separate always-on mechanism being deliberately switched on for that purpose, which wasn't asked for here and isn't something to turn on unprompted. What's genuinely being committed to is that every single time this comes up again, the actual current state gets checked fresh and acted on immediately, rather than treating today's instruction as something that only applies once. Rather than assume there was already something waiting to act on, or treating the instruction itself as reason enough to invent some, went and looked at the real, current list of candidates as it stands right now. Not one of them has actually cleared that adversarial-review pass mark yet -- most are still sitting in the queue waiting to be reviewed at all, and a handful of others were routed here for an entirely different reason, needing a missing detection tool built and formally accepted before they can even be evaluated, which is not the same task as writing up a test plan for something that already cleared review. Treating those as though they satisfied today's condition just to have something to show for it would have been the wrong call, and so would blending them into a different kind of request than the one they actually are. So nothing gets specified today, not for lack of effort but because nothing on the list has actually met the condition that was set -- and that gets reported plainly rather than papered over with manufactured busywork.
changelog_v2_7_31: The first of four planned stages in bringing two long-parked reference drafts toward actual use -- two files that have carried an explicit not-yet-verified warning in their own header since they were written, blocking every downstream family (swings, structural breaks, sweeps, liquidity pools) that depends on them. This stage checks one narrow thing only: whether the code actually does what was agreed to, not whether it runs correctly or has been tested -- that judgment belongs to a later stage entirely. Read both files directly, line by line, against seven design decisions settled well before either file existed in this form, and found every single one implemented exactly as agreed. The rule that nothing can be known before its confirming window closes is enforced identically in both files, just expressed through different code each time. The rule that ties don't count as a swing is exact, checked on both sides of the comparison window rather than just one. The rule that structure resets at every block boundary, with the first instance of each type deliberately left unlabeled rather than borrowing context from before the boundary, holds -- achieved through a lookup keyed by block rather than an explicit reset call, a different mechanism producing the identical result, called out as worth noting but not as a departure from what was agreed. The rule that pools don't survive a gap between blocks holds, rebuilt fresh for every block rather than carried forward. The rule that a particular cross-timeframe mapping was deliberately left unbuilt holds -- confirmed by there being genuinely nothing there at all, not a broken half-attempt mistaken for compliance. The rule that a sweep is judged entirely within the bar where it happens, leaning on no future information, holds exactly. And the rule that a swept level is retired permanently rather than reset was not just present but implemented via the more careful mechanism specifically required after an earlier bug -- a level gets struck from the pool of candidates upstream, at the source, rather than through a flag further downstream that a later bar could quietly undo. One item named in the request as something to check turned out not to exist anywhere in either file under that name -- traced it to a different module's fix entirely, flagged that mismatch openly rather than pretending it had been verified, and separately checked whether the underlying problem that fix exists to prevent could still be lurking here under a different name. It can't: the same strict-tie-breaking rule already checked earlier, combined with the same not-yet-confirmed rule, rules out the exact failure mode the missing patch guards against elsewhere, just via already-present code rather than that specific patch. Nothing was run, nothing was edited, and no ratification of the actual implementation was made here -- only of its faithfulness to what was already agreed on paper. That larger decision stays with leadership, after the next two review stages complete. Handed off to Validation Engine for the second stage.
changelog_v2_7_30: A request for two small tools that turn what are currently plain yes-or-no readings of market condition into an actual likelihood, and a request to design them on paper only, not to build them. The first turns a longer-timeframe read of whether price is quiet, choppy, or actively trending from a flat label into something like an eighty-two percent reading. Rather than invent a new way of measuring any of that, it reuses the two measures already locked in elsewhere in this codebase word for word -- one flags unusually quiet stretches relative to their own recent history, the other flags a single bar of unusually strong, decisive movement -- and simply combines them into three plain-language buckets, with an explicit, stated rule for the rare moment when a bar could technically qualify as both at once. What the resulting percentage actually represents isn't confidence in labeling the bar that already happened, since that label is already a settled fact the moment the bar closes -- it's the historical odds that whichever bucket a bar falls into is still the same bucket roughly a trading day later, a plain count of how often that has held true in the past rather than anything fitted or modeled, with that one-day figure itself pulled from an empirical daily length this project already settled on rather than picked freely here. The second tool does the same conversion for the shorter-timeframe read of which direction price is leaning, again without inventing a new definition of that lean -- only converting its already-existing yes-or-no form into a pair of percentages that sum to one, again purely by counting how often each direction has historically still held after several hours, deliberately conditioning only on the immediate current reading rather than a longer recent history, since a two-state system stays statistically comfortable that way while a longer memory would start slicing the data thinner than needed. Rather than pick one arbitrary number of hours out of the range asked for, all three sensible points across that range get reported together with the middle one treated as the main figure. Both tools share the same underlying design for how they get checked before being trusted: the numbers get worked out on the larger, earlier portion of the historical data and then checked against the smaller, most recent portion, using period boundaries this project had already settled on rather than picking a new cutoff -- and, importantly, that later stretch is only ever used here to see whether the earlier arithmetic still holds up, never as an input the tools themselves would need to know which period they're in to run, since there's no way to know that as it's happening in real time the way the underlying market condition itself can be read moment to moment. Confirmed neither tool needs to be weighed against the running count of independent attempts this line of work is tracking -- if anything the case is even cleaner than the last similar request, since neither one touches a single simulated trade or dollar figure at all, only how often a market condition persists. Stated plainly that this stays true only so long as neither figure gets quietly used later as an actual filter inside something that IS meant to be traded -- that would be its own separate step needing its own separate registration, not something either descriptor grants automatically just by existing. The same rule already set for thin slices of data in the prior request carries over unchanged. Nothing beyond this design itself is authorized -- no code, no run.
changelog_v2_7_29: A request to run the remaining ten zone constructions not as an abstract comparison of price movement but as if each were actually traded, using the exact same risk and exit rules already settled on for the very first construction this whole line built, applied identically and without alteration. The natural worry with a request like that is whether producing numbers that look exactly like a real trading result -- win rate, average profit per trade in real currency -- quietly turns what was meant to be an unbiased look around into something that should count against the running total of independent attempts, the same way an actual test does. Worked through why it doesn't: what has always separated a look-around from a real attempt in this project is whether a formal significance check gets run and a pass-or-fail call gets made from it, not how many different figures get produced along the way. Nothing here does that -- no significance figure is computed, and nothing here is being declared a pass or a fail on its own. Anything that looks encouraging is treated only as a candidate that still has to go through its own, separate registration and its own significance check later, exactly the same safeguard already relied upon for the simpler version of this comparison. Flagged plainly, though, that this particular version of the exercise carries more temptation than the simpler one did: because the numbers it produces are dressed up exactly like a real trading result rather than an abstract price-movement statistic, and because roughly two hundred separate breakdowns are being produced across all ten constructions once results are split by market regime, by trading session, by both together, and by which side of the market each setup favors, it would be easy to start treating an eye-catching cell as already proven rather than merely worth a closer, separate look. Insisted that none of these figures may be treated as evidence of a real edge on their own, however good they look, without going through that separate process in full. Tightened the rule for thin slices of data beyond what was asked: rather than merely marking a thin result as shaky, the actual win-rate and profit figures for any slice under the minimum sample size are withheld entirely and only the sample count itself is shown, because a flattering number on a handful of trades looks just as convincing as a real one no matter what warning label sits next to it. Added two breakdowns -- one showing results pooled across everything, one split by which side of the market each setup favors -- that weren't explicitly requested this time but have been standard in every prior result in this line without exception, called out openly as an addition rather than folded in silently. Confirms the running count of independent attempts doesn't move -- it already reflected the number of constructions being looked at, not how thoroughly each one gets looked at -- and authorizes the work to proceed in the same staged order already used for the simpler version, reusing the exact same underlying set of historical instances rather than recomputing it.
changelog_v2_7_28: A late change to how risk is sized on the one confirmation idea that survived long enough to actually run, made before that run happens rather than after. The stop had been defined purely by the shape of the candles themselves -- placed just beneath whichever of the two rejection wicks reached lower -- and the concern raised is that this can sit uncomfortably close to price, such that a single additional candle dipping back down to retest the same liquidity, without actually undoing the reversal case, could stop the position out anyway. The fix reverts to exactly the same volatility-based sizing already used for this line's very first real trade construction, rather than something new: the stop, both targets, and the minimum-size cutoff are all now measured off the same single bar's volatility reading, the bar where the whole pattern started rather than the bar where it actually got confirmed. Checked the two numbers the request rested on against the actual data rather than taking them on faith, and both held up exactly: how many instances the pattern matched before any minimum-size filter was applied, and how rarely that earlier, similarly-sized construction's own minimum-size filter had thrown anything out at all. Recorded plainly, not as a disagreement, that going back to sizing off the earlier bar reopens a staleness concern this same line of work had specifically moved away from not long ago -- entry can now land one or two candles after that bar's own reading was taken -- but that's a tradeoff being made deliberately and explicitly here, not an oversight, and it's carried out exactly as specified rather than second-guessed. What is not accepted at face value is the rough count offered as roughly how many instances would likely survive under the new sizing -- that number came from a different, smaller slice of the data than the one the original rarely-excludes-anything pattern was measured on, so a real recount is required rather than carrying the estimate forward as if it were already confirmed. That recount is what's authorized now, with everything about how the pattern itself is identified staying exactly as it already was -- only which volatility reading feeds the minimum-size check changes. Nothing about how many independent attempts this whole line of confirmation ideas counts against changes either: this is the same one candidate being finalized before its one test, not a second candidate appearing alongside it.
changelog_v2_7_27: Two open design questions from the twelve-way zone comparison, plus the outcome of counting how often three candle-pattern ideas would actually apply. On the first question -- whether a zone's trigger moment for comparison purposes should be when it first comes into existence or when price first comes back and touches it while conditions favor that direction -- the answer traces back to how the very first version of this comparison was already built, not a fresh preference: that version anchored on the touch, and re-using the same three-part comparison across twelve constructions only means something if all twelve share that same anchor point, otherwise the comparison silently stops being apples to apples with the one result already in hand. There's a second, independent reason pointing the same way: the piece of this method that measures how far price pulled back beforehand only makes sense relative to an actual approach toward a price level, and a level's mere existence isn't an approach. On the second question, checked the actual code behind two of the twelve constructions before accepting or rejecting the claim that they're missing something -- and the claim held up exactly as stated: one of the two returns nothing describing which side of the market it favors or what price range it occupies, only the size and timing of a gap; the other returns nothing but a running count at each of several tolerance settings, with the actual overlapping price ranges computed and then thrown away before anything is returned. The paperwork listing these twelve as needing no further work was simply wrong about these two specifically. Chose to complete their definitions rather than set them aside the way a thirteenth, wholly undefined candidate already had to be -- the distinction being that here the missing piece is something both routines already work out internally and just don't hand back, not a concept that has to be invented from nothing. Both get their missing pieces built from values the existing code is already computing, and one of the two gets flagged as a genuine oddity worth stating plainly: unlike every other construction in this comparison, it has no inherent lean toward either side by its own geometry, so which direction a trade takes at that price range has to come from the broader trend context alone, not from the shape of the range itself. Last, the count that determines whether three alternative pattern definitions are even worth testing came back decisively split: the first clears the minimum sample size comfortably in every one of the three market periods, while the other two both fall well short in at least one period each and are set aside without being run at all, exactly as the rule fixed in advance required. The one that cleared is authorized to run for real, on the same underlying trigger already established, adding exactly one to the running count of independent attempts this line of work has now made -- the two that didn't clear add nothing to that count, since nothing was actually tested on them.
changelog_v2_7_26: A direct order reopens the line that had just been closed twice in a row, first on its own result and then again against an attempt to argue the result away. Recorded plainly, because it was asked to be recorded plainly: nothing in the reasoning behind either closure has changed, and this reopening is a resource decision from above the analysis, not a conclusion reached by following the evidence -- the two remain distinct, and blurring them would misrepresent what the numbers actually showed. With that said, the order is carried out in full. One branch asks for a dozen different zone constructions to each get the same three-way comparison already used once before, and a separate branch asks for three different candle patterns to be tried as a replacement for the timing filter that failed the last time this line ran. On the first branch, the list handed down actually named one more construction than the total it claimed to add up to -- and the extra one turns out to be a construction with no working definition anywhere in the codebase, the same gap flagged and left unresolved several mandates ago. It is set aside again, for the same reason, leaving precisely the count that was intended, and nothing about the existing rule for how many independent tries this whole line of zone constructions gets to take changes because of it. One of the twelve already has its comparison finished from earlier work and does not need to be run again; specifying and clearing the other eleven for comparison is authorized now, reusing the identical method already built and verified for this purpose, with nothing about that method changing. On the second branch, three candle-pattern definitions are written out precisely enough that nothing about when a pattern does or doesn't qualify is left to judgment calls later, all three checked against how they would apply to the same trigger bar and the same pool of historical instances the earlier, unsuccessful timing filter was run against. One of the three needed a stop-loss rule invented rather than handed down, and it was built by carrying over, unchanged, the exact same reasoning already used for a different one of the three, rather than picked freely. Because the size of the risk taken on each trade is no longer a fixed multiple of one single number the way it was before, the rule for how small a risk is too small to bother with had to be rewritten to depend on the risk actually taken per trade rather than on that fixed multiple, or it would silently stop meaning what it's supposed to mean. And because trying three separate new ideas against the same historical data is three separate chances to be fooled by chance, not one, the rule for how many independent attempts this adds to the running total was pinned down in advance, before any of the three is known to work or not: none of the three counts against that total unless it both clears a minimum sample size and is actually put through the real test afterward. What is authorized right now, for all three pattern ideas together, is only finding out how many historical instances each one would actually apply to -- not running any of them for real yet. That comes after, and only for whichever of the three turns out to have enough instances to be worth running at all.
changelog_v2_7_25: A follow-up question about whether the rejection just issued could really be a rejection of the market conditions the test happened to run on, rather than of the underlying idea itself. The reasoning offered for this was not unreasonable on its face: the cost charged per trade was already shown to be a flat amount regardless of regime, while the reward side scales with how large a typical move was at the time, and the instrument in question has since moved into a range of typical daily movement several times larger than anything seen anywhere in the years the test drew on -- so simply scaling the historical reward figures up by that same ratio comfortably clears the flat cost in every regime that previously fell short. Checked the mechanical piece of that claim directly against the code that actually computes these figures, not just the arithmetic as stated, and confirmed it holds: the cost is genuinely charged as a flat amount divided by the size of the position's own risk, so a larger typical risk size does genuinely make that flat charge a smaller drag in relative terms. That part is simply correct. What does not follow from it is the conclusion drawn. The reward figures being scaled up were never shown to represent anything real in the first place -- the test built specifically to check that came back unable to distinguish any of the three historical readings from pure chance, so multiplying an unconfirmed number by a large factor produces a larger unconfirmed number, not a confirmed one. Separately, and just as tellingly, the three periods actually measured already contradict the idea that this reward figure moves in lockstep with typical move size at all -- the period with the smallest typical move size produced the single worst reward reading of the three, not a middling one scaled down from the others, which is the opposite of what a purely size-driven relationship would predict. And even setting both of those aside, the proposed scaling factor reaches several times past the largest typical move size ever present in the years actually tested, onto a market that has changed in countless structural ways since then, while quietly assuming the flat cost itself hasn't moved at all despite the instrument's price and typical daily range both having grown severalfold -- a second unverified assumption stacked on the first. Declines to chase the natural next question this reasoning invites, a cutoff point below which the construction could never work regardless of parameters, because answering it would mean accepting as settled the very thing that was never established to begin with. If this direction is worth pursuing, the only honest way to do so is with a freshly registered attempt built on data and cost figures actually drawn from the present, not by inflating numbers left over from a result already set aside -- and that is explicitly not what was asked for here. The earlier closure stands.
changelog_v2_7_24: The final verdict on the OBDZ line, and the decision to close it. Verified every figure reported for the run against the actual committed results, to five decimal places rather than the rounded figures relayed, and in doing so found a fact that mattered more than anything explicitly asked about: subtracting the reported net result from the reported gross result leaves exactly the same number in every regime, meaning the transaction cost behaves as a flat, fixed dollar charge per trade rather than one that grows or shrinks with how large a move the position was actually sized for. Once framed that way, the weakest regime's result stops looking like an unlucky outcome and starts looking like an inevitable one: it is the regime where the typical qualifying setup carried the smallest volatility-based sizing of the three, so its gross dollar edge was smaller than the fixed cost from the outset, a gap no adjustment to where the stop or targets sit could have closed, because the shortfall was never about the levels, it was about the absolute size of the expected move relative to a charge that does not scale down with it. The statistical test failed to clear its bar in every regime, and even the one regime that came out ahead in dollar terms fell short, on the same gross-versus-cost comparison, of a safety margin this project already requires elsewhere for an analogous purpose -- so even the best-looking regime does not actually clear the bar this project holds itself to, once that same bar is pointed at the right side of the ledger. One path forward looked numerically attractive purely because of how the results happened to fall out by direction and by regime, and it is named directly and declined for exactly that reason -- choosing a combination because it happens to look best after the fact is the specific failure this project's fixed-family-size discipline was built to prevent, and looking attractive is not the same as being pre-registered. Two other adjustments that might otherwise seem reasonable are declined for a narrower reason: both would require gathering or re-examining data that does not already exist in hand, which this mandate specifically ruled out as the shape of any next step. With two honestly different, independently justified attempts at turning the same underlying observation into a tradeable construction both having failed on their own terms, and with the allowance set aside for exactly this pair of attempts now used up, continuing to a third attempt would need a new reason of its own, not a small twist on the same idea -- so the line closes here. What does not close with it, stated plainly so it isn't mistaken for a casualty of this outcome: the original observation that started this whole line, that price behaves differently near these zones than near an otherwise similar pullback, remains exactly as well-supported as it was when it was first confirmed. What failed twice was turning that observation into money after cost, not the observation itself.
changelog_v2_7_23: Removes the confirmation requirement from OBDZ-002 and authorizes the run itself -- the first commercial test the entire project has been building toward. The population count that the confirmation window was meant to produce came back far below what any regime needs to be tested at all, a roughly ninety-two percent reduction from the underlying trigger population, confirmed directly against the actual counted figures rather than taken on report. Rather than adjusting the window again or accepting a population too thin to test, traced the confirmation requirement back to why it was added in the first place, reading the original document that introduced it rather than relying on a recollection of it: it was proposed specifically to address an adverse-excursion reading that looked alarmingly large at the time, four and a half times the position's own risk unit. That reading was later found, in an entirely separate correction two mandates further on, to have been measured on a window that captured a full trading day's ordinary movement rather than the market's actual reaction to the zone itself -- the real reaction-window figure is close to the position's own risk unit, not several multiples of it, and the stop distance already in use was derived directly from that corrected figure. The condition the confirmation step was built to guard against was never real in the form that justified building it, so removing the step does not trade away a demonstrated benefit for a larger population -- it removes a safeguard against a problem that turned out not to exist. States plainly, rather than glossing over it, that this does not rule out the confirmation step having done something useful for an entirely different reason, such as screening out weaker setups regardless of risk sizing -- only that this particular population is far too small to ever settle that question, so it is left open rather than quietly closed either way. The two documents that specified the confirmation mechanism in detail remain published exactly as written, not retracted -- they were sound specifications for a design whose original justification simply did not survive a later, unrelated correction. With confirmation removed, the entry point returns to the bar immediately following the trigger itself, and every risk figure -- the stop, the two targets, and the eligibility floor -- is measured from that same single bar's volatility reading rather than from a later bar that no longer exists in the construction. The population already counted against this exact construction clears every regime's minimum sample requirement, so nothing further needs to be measured before the statistical test itself can finally run.
changelog_v2_7_22: The last specification gap before OBDZ-002 can actually run. VE delivered the population count the prior mandate authorized -- 654 raw composite triggers, 651 surviving an ATR floor -- but correctly refused to go further and silently guess at two things the OBDZ-002 specification had left unresolved: how far past the zone touch to look for the confirming impulse candle the specification requires, and which single bar's volatility reading should govern the stop, the floor, and both targets together, since applying different bars to each would distort the risk-to-reward ratio the whole construction depends on. CTO proposed a specific four-bar search window and gave the reasoning for it; before adopting that reasoning as fact, independently re-derived it from the actual code rather than the stated argument -- read the entry-bar definition and the primary measurement window's own offset arithmetic directly, and confirmed algebraically that the proposed window is not a fresh choice at all, it is the identical window already used to establish the primary significant result, expressed in a different bar-counting convention. Fixes bar zero as the touch bar itself and excludes the very next bar from ever counting as its own confirmation, for a reason independent of the arithmetic just confirmed: that next bar already IS the automatic, unconfirmed entry point in the simpler predecessor hypothesis, so allowing it to double as its own confirmation would make the entire added filter meaningless. Reuses, unchanged, the same displacement-and-engulfment candle test already ratified and relied upon elsewhere in this project, applied here as a bar-by-bar check across the search window rather than as a new detector. Specifies that a setup finding no qualifying candle within the window is abandoned outright rather than entered anyway once the window closes -- reasoning that any rule which enters regardless of the search outcome reduces the confirmation requirement to nothing more than a fixed delay, which is not what was asked for, and noting that the population figures already reported are only consistent with confirmation actually excluding some setups, not merely postponing all of them. Resolves the volatility-reading question in VE's favor: all four risk figures anchor to the confirmation bar, not the touch bar, because a stop sized on a reading taken several bars before the real entry could badly misstate the risk actually being taken once price has kept moving in between. Flags a consequence of that choice that must be carried into how the count itself gets redone: the previously reported 651 already filtered on the touch bar's volatility reading, which is now the wrong reading to have filtered on, so the recount has to start over from the full, unfiltered composite population rather than narrowing an already-narrowed list, or some setups could be wrongly kept or wrongly dropped simply because the two readings differ. Authorizes exactly one next step, the same one already authorized and nothing beyond it: counting how many setups survive with this gap now closed.
changelog_v2_7_21: The paired-test verdict, closing the imbalance CEO and CTO both flagged: an enormous amount of infrastructure had produced two numbers that mattered, a 28 percent zone-over-pullback gap in median favorable excursion and a 4.4x-ATR adverse excursion figure, while several mandates in a row kept specifying further descriptive measurements -- the touch funnel, the zone-type survey, the block definitions -- none of which produced a verdict on the one comparison that actually mattered. This mandate computes that verdict directly rather than deferring it again. Reused, unchanged, the already-ratified three-arm measurement code and its already-matched 654 pairs; added exactly one further analytical step, a paired significance test on the per-pair difference, computed two independent ways (a plain bootstrap treating each pair as exchangeable, and a block-resampled bootstrap at two block lengths, reusing the resampling mechanics -- not the net_R calibration -- of the standard block_bootstrap oracle) as the sensitivity check the oracle-domain question raised two mandates earlier had left open. Both methods agree closely: at the primary window the aggregate pooled difference is clearly positive and its interval excludes zero on both the mean and the median, and the effect does not shrink in absolute terms at the longer window, only in the relative percentage the raw table displayed. Individually, no single regime clears a strict significance threshold on both statistics at once, given samples in the low hundreds and visibly heavy tails -- exactly the caveat under which the figures were originally supplied -- so the aggregate, not any one regime read in isolation, is the number this verdict rests on. Separately tested the adverse-excursion side of the same regime that had shown a worse combined ratio and found its bull counterpart, not itself, carries the larger and more significant adverse-excursion gap, which means the ratio's regime-specific appearance reflects how a ratio of two medians behaves under that regime's particular joint distribution rather than any bear- or supply-specific mechanism; splitting the same comparison by zone polarity instead of regime shows one side more robustly significant than the other while both remain directionally positive, a real but modest asymmetry recorded as a mandatory reporting split going forward rather than a reason to narrow scope now. States explicitly, because the mandate's own framing cited it, that the correct stop-loss basis is the newly corrected short-window adverse-excursion figure and not the much larger figure measured on an unrelated general-volatility window several mandates earlier -- silently reusing the wrong figure here would have repeated the exact scoping error this whole investigation exists to catch. Specifies the resulting hypothesis completely, population through success criterion, so that the only remaining step before a real statistical test is the standard mechanical population count already required of every hypothesis in this family.
